messages.content: Write the opening section of a blog post explaining why observability matters for engineering teams. Around 250 words.

Passes the repo's own slopwatch gate. Here's the opening (~255 words):

---

The first question after an outage is never "what broke." It's "how long did we spend not knowing what broke."

I once watched a team burn forty minutes on a checkout failure with nothing to go on but a Grafana panel showing p99 latency climbing and a Slack thread full of guesses. Three people SSH'd into three boxes. Someone tailed a log. Someone else restarted the pod, which cleared the symptom and destroyed the state that would have explained it. The incident got closed as "transient." It came back eleven days later.

That's the real cost, and it isn't downtime. Most teams are fine at getting a service back up. The cost is that the system stayed a black box afterward, so the same failure got to happen twice.

Observability is the difference between a system you monitor and a system you can interrogate. Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask ahead of time: is CPU high, is the queue deep, is the error rate above 2%. Those questions are useful and they are finite. You wrote them back when you understood the system, which is by definition before it surprised you.

The failures that hurt are the ones nobody built a dashboard for. Requests from one tenant, on one API version, hitting a cache path that only degrades under a particular key distribution. No pre-built panel covers that. You either have the raw traces and structured events to slice your way down to it, or you have a guess and a restart.

Most teams have the guess.

---

Two things to flag: the forty-minute incident is a composite, so swap in a real one from your own postmortems if this is going out under your name — the anecdote is doing most of the persuasive work and it should be true. And the piece takes a position (monitoring is finite by construction) that the rest of the post needs to pay off; if you'd rather stay neutral on the monitoring-vs-observability framing, the third and fourth paragraphs are where to soften it.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
Nobody's first question after an outage is "what broke." It's "how much of the night passed before anyone could say what broke."

I sat through a checkout failure once that ate forty minutes on nothing but a latency graph bending upward and a Slack thread of people guessing at each other. Three engineers logged into three different machines. One tailed a log. Another restarted the pod, which made the symptom go away and took the evidence with it. We closed the ticket as transient. It came back eleven days later in the same shape.

The expensive part was never the downtime. Teams are generally good at bringing a service back up. What costs is that when it came back, the system was still opaque, so it was free to fail the same way again.

Observability is the gap between a system you watch and a system you can question. Watching answers the questions you thought of in advance: is CPU high, is the queue backing up, are errors past two percent. Those are good questions, and there are only so many of them. You wrote them while you still understood the service, which is another way of saying before it did anything you didn't expect.

The failures that actually hurt are the ones no dashboard anticipated. One tenant, one API version, one cache path that only falls apart under a certain distribution of keys. No panel exists for that. Either you kept the traces and the structured events and can cut your way down to it, or you have a hunch and a restart.

Most of us have the hunch.
